title: C-130 carrier fix pass
script:
October 1963. The North Atlantic. A four-engine cargo plane is lining up to land on an aircraft carrier. No tailhook. No arresting wire. Nothing to catch it.

This is a C-130 Hercules. Its wings are 132 feet wide. A carrier deck was never built for anything this big. And the Navy wants to know one thing: can a plane this size deliver cargo straight to a ship in the middle of the ocean?

The pilot is Lieutenant James Flatley the Third. The ship is the USS Forrestal, 500 miles off Boston. The sea is rough. The wind is 40 knots across the deck.

Flatley lines up on the centerline. His right wingtip will pass the carrier's island with less than 15 feet to spare. One gust, and the wing hits the tower.

He brings it down. The Hercules slams onto the deck, the propellers reverse, and the giant stops in just 267 feet.

Then he takes off again. No catapult. Just four engines at full power and the end of the deck.

He does it again. And again. 29 touch-and-goes. 21 full-stop landings. 21 takeoffs. At weights up to 121,000 pounds.

It works. On paper, it's the perfect carrier delivery plane. It can carry far more, and fly far farther, than the Navy's own carrier transport.

But the Navy says no. Too big. Too risky for a crowded deck, every single day.

Flatley gets the Distinguished Flying Cross. And no C-130 has landed on a carrier since.

That exact plane survives. Today it sits in the National Naval Aviation Museum in Pensacola, Florida.

Some things aren't in the manual. Somebody had to write them first.

C130.description: Photorealistic reference of a 1963 United States Marine Corps KC-130F Hercules, Lockheed C-130 family. Four-engine high-wing turboprop transport, four-blade propellers, black rounded nose radome, chunky fuselage with an upswept rear section and cargo ramp. CONVENTIONAL TAIL: one tall vertical fin with the horizontal stabilizers mounted LOW at the base of the fin, level with the rear fuselage. It is NOT a T-tail - nothing on top of the fin. Light gull-grey upper and white lower paint, refueling pods under the outer wings. Clean three-quarter front view on a plain light grey background, no text, no watermark.

shots.image_prompt_full: Photorealistic vertical shot, 1963 color film look. Seen from behind and slightly above: the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules (conventional low tail, horizontal stabilizers at the base of the fin, not a T-tail) on final approach just above the stern of a huge grey 1960s aircraft carrier in the rough North Atlantic, landing gear down, flaps down, a few meters above the end of the flight deck. Choppy dark sea, overcast sky. Tense, realistic, no text.
shots.motion_prompt: The C-130 descends steadily toward the carrier deck, wings rocking slightly in the gusty wind, propellers spinning, the ship pitching in the waves. Camera follows from behind and slightly above. No fire, no explosion.

shots.image_prompt_full: Photorealistic vertical low-angle shot from the carrier deck looking up at the rear of the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules passing just overhead: upswept rear fuselage, closed cargo ramp, no tailhook, conventional tail with low horizontal stabilizers at the base of the fin. Overcast sky. 1963 color film look, realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical side shot of the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules flying low over a dark North Atlantic ocean, four propellers spinning, conventional tail with horizontal stabilizers low at the base of the fin (not a T-tail), overcast sky. 1963 color film look, realistic, no text.

shots.image_prompt_full: Photorealistic vertical aerial view looking straight down at a 1960s aircraft carrier flight deck at sea, with the large grey-and-white C-130 Hercules parked on the deck, its long wings stretching almost the full width of the deck, small jets and sailors around it for scale. Realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical shot from the carrier deck: the long right wing and spinning propellers of the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules sweeping past the carrier's tall grey island superstructure with only a few meters of clearance, sailors ducking. Conventional low tail visible. Tense, realistic, 1963 color film look, no text.

Photorealistic vertical shot from the side on the carrier deck: the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules (conventional low tail, not a T-tail) touching down on the grey flight deck, main wheels on the deck with light grey tire smoke, four propellers spinning, rough sea behind. 1963 color film look, realistic, no text.
shots.motion_prompt: The C-130 touches down firmly on the carrier deck with light grey tire smoke only, rolls forward and decelerates quickly as the propellers reverse, deck crew watching. No fire, no flames, no explosion. Camera stays steady on the deck.

shots.image_prompt_full: Photorealistic vertical shot: the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules stopped on the carrier flight deck seen from the side, conventional tail with low horizontal stabilizers, propellers still turning, flight deck crew in colored jerseys running toward it, open sea and grey sky beyond the deck edge. 1963 color film look, realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical shot from the side of the carrier deck: the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules lifting off from the bow of the aircraft carrier at full power, nose up, wheels just leaving the deck, conventional low tail, spray and open ocean ahead, deck crew watching. 1963 color film look, realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical side view at golden late-afternoon light: the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules flying low alongside an aircraft carrier for another pass, conventional low tail clearly visible, long ship wake on the sea, dramatic clouds. Realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical close-up of the hands of a 1960s US Navy officer in dark dress uniform opening a small dark blue presentation box, soft dramatic light, the medal inside out of focus and not identifiable. Realistic, no text.

Photorealistic vertical shot of the grey-and-white C-130 Hercules on display inside a large bright aviation museum hangar, side view showing the conventional low tail, polished floor, visitors looking up at it for scale. Realistic, no readable text.
